cards.title: I'm sorry, but you still have to think

depth.text: someone tested **AI rewrites** and found developers still **need to think** about the trade-offs

DHH asked an LLM to move **Campfire Once** from Ruby on Rails to Rust, then also tried Elixir and Go. At 100 POSTs/s, Rust delivered ~14% of events and Elixir ~60%, but Elixir timed out on ~23% of HTTP POST requests. The article argues that delivery rate alone misses **trade-offs** like latency, memory use, and whether slow clients should be disconnected.
data: Rust successful notification delivery under heavy load
Elixir HTTP POST requests timed out at 100 POSTs/s
Elixir memory use during 100 req/s stress test

cards.camps: Two camps: some say developers still need to review generated code and understand the system; others think this may go the way of compiler output, or that low-stakes work doesn't need exhaustive scrutiny.

comments.text: This article just reminds me that workslop is so hard to counter because it takes no effort to produce and immense effort to debunk
It's worth noting that the context here is a system that was translated by an LLM which is the ideal use case for it. 90% of the thinking had already been done by developers of the existing system.

You need to understand the system you're working on enough to make well-informed decisions about its current and future states. In some cases you can get away with not reading the code. And maybe in the future that will be more common. But for now, I personally prefer to read (or skim) the code, and not abdicate to AI.

Most of this article went over my head, but I think this is key point: if your prompt is not specific enough, many decisions are a coin flip. If you are using AI, you still have to know what you want it to do. If you are a project manager and give your team incomplete requirements, the result may not be unlike this.

cards.title: Terence Tao: Math 2.0 [pdf]

depth.text: Terence Tao asks how **AI** could change **the work and purpose of mathematicians**

Tao's slide warns that reaching open problems too soon with automated tools could **sterilize the surrounding field**. One commenter compares pure math to a **shared codebase**: a proof can solve a problem yet still need rebuilding before it fits existing theory.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the cancer example overlooks that medicines can lack understood mechanisms; others say Tao is thinking ahead about AI's effect on human work, not arguing against AI.

comments.text: I work in drug discovery and AI and his slide about cancer medicine isn't very well informed. We have models and narratives about how drugs work, but they are woefully incomplete. I ask nearly every doctor/researched in the medical field: if you had a AI-created drug that tremendously improved cancer treatment outcomes for your patient, would you hesitate to prescribe it because nobody understood…

Explaining Tao's point in software terms: the point of pure mathematics is to build and maintain a high quality "codebase" of theory, definitions and proofs. "Open problems are lighthouses not destinations" mean that these are currently not well explained by the theories and people should look into extending the codebase on that direction. The current generation of math AI is not a "good citizen"…

> Before injecting this cocktail into your bloodstream, would you want to know that there is at least one human cancer researcher who understands the mechanism behind this cure. Tao is out of his lane; lots of medicines don't have understood mechanisms. We don't even have the mechanisms behind general anesthesia nailed down; do you want to forgo it when the docs cut you open to remove your tumors?

Slide 12 and 13 sum up my conclusions from the Oct 8 100+ reactions to 100+ solutions. Several reported OpenAI drop included answers put a wrap on problems they had been working for years. Several said that they have to completely rewrite grant requests that they had just submitted. Others described learning of the solutions problems they had been working on like losing an old friend or a lover…

If you have not been following and focus on the cancer slide as an anti AI take, Tao has been involved and has a positive attitude towards AI for a while, he is just thinking a bit ahead on how the work of humans might change. https://teorth.github.io/tao-web/ai-views.html

cards.title: C for Rust programmers

depth.text: someone wrote a guide to the **C quirks** that catch **Rust programmers** off guard
The author walks through how C strings end with a **null byte**, **arrays become pointers** when passed to functions, and **error handling** is left to the programmer.

cards.camps: Two camps: the article urges checking malloc for a null result; one commenter says overcommit often means running out of memory won't produce one, though invalid arguments still can.

comments.text: Any tutorial for C should explain compiler warnings and other tools that help make code safer. In C, you do not rely on the language specification but on tooling. Especially for Rust programmers, this needs to be explained more explicitly. And of course, you can build abstractions using types in C. So a tutorial should also focus on that, and perhaps not start with a low-level string reversal…

There is a nuanced mistake in > If your machine runs out of memory, reversed[i] will cause a segfault upon being accessed. In order to avoid unhelpful segfaults, the program should check for a null pointer and gracefully exit if one is found If overcommit is enabled (often by default), malloc will not return null when machine runs out of memory. malloc will still return null if input argument is…

Re: arrays are pointers. One of my favorite things to show just how bare this is in C is to show array access commutativity. char c = {1,2,3}
c[1] == *(c + 1)
*(c + 1) == *(1 + c)
c[1] == 1[c]
C is wonderfully simple at times.

Some fun quirks I never learned until years after first getting into C: - zero-initialization via `= {0};` will still leave padding and any data not covered by the smallest elements of unions uninitialized, so serializing data structures zeroed via that method is unsafe - A pointer that increments any more than 1 past the end of a valid memory region (e.g. the end of a buffer) is instant…

My biggest bewilderment with C is that malloc has to store the buffer size otherwise free could not work...but nobody in decades thought to make this information accessible to the programmer! If you want to keep track of buffer bounds in C, you have to do it artisanally. Despite it's, in most implementations, stored right there next to the data and thus in L1 cache already.

cards.title: Why DuckDB 2.0 is faster

depth.text: someone found **DuckDB reads data from S3** much faster, without changing the query

For a query reading one column from a 2.2 GB Parquet file, the writer’s M5 laptop took **18.8 s** with DuckDB 1.5.5 and **7.7 s** with the 2.0 alpha. A separate pool of download threads fetches row groups ahead, so workers can decode while downloads continue.
data: One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 1.5.5
One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 2.0 alpha

comments.text: Great visualization. Side note their new c++ extension api is also gonna be faster from the perspective of development / distribution of those extensions

Here's a 2025 article about how elegantly that can handle what is otherwise quite a challenging class of query for your typical RDBMS: https://duckdb.org/2025/10/22/duckdb-graph-queries-duckpgq

I wish more database engines used a Task-based design like Umbra / CedarDB. Most of the DB engines out there still seem to use a "n-threads" style parallelism with exchange operations and poor async I/O management. DuckDB is improving on this front, but in some sense is catching up to R&D (and implementation!) that is now decades old. A "rhetorical challenge" I like to give software developers…

cards.title: Nix wrote half of my debugger

glossary.debug symbols: Extra information that lets a debugger connect a program's running state to its source code.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.deterministic: Something that gives the same result when it gets the same input.
glossary.open model: An AI model shared for others to use, though “open” can mean different things.
glossary.M&A: Mergers and acquisitions: when companies combine or one company buys another.
glossary.acquihiring: Buying a company mainly to bring its employees onto your team.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.diffusion model: An image-making AI that starts with visual noise and gradually turns it into a picture.
